mainTopic: A sharecropper (מְקַבֵּל) who takes a field for a few years versus seven years: planting פשתן, cutting קורות שקמה, and whether he is paid for the שבח (growth) of the sycamore when he leaves.
overview: The משנה teaches that someone who takes a field for only a few years may not plant flax, which weakens the soil, and may not cut the sycamore branches used for beams. With a seven-year deal he may do both. אביי says the short-term worker is still paid for the sycamore's growth (שבח), and רבא says he is not. The גמרא challenges רבא from ברייתות about a court appraisal. In the end it shows that only a buyer at the יובל keeps the growth, because he was a true owner and a special פסוק gives it to him. Then come real cases: רב פפא is paid for palm trees that sprouted in his hay field only as wood, and רב ביבי gets nothing because he lost nothing. רב יוסף tries to remove his dead planter's five heirs, but the ruling that heirs leave with no payment is rejected. A planter who promised to leave if he caused a loss leads to a three-way argument, and רבא calls the promise an אסמכתא that is not binding. The amud ends with רבא approving רבינא's removal of his planter without warning, and it begins quoting רבא's rule about such workers, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Short-term sharecropper: no flax, no sycamore beams
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that someone who takes a field for only a few years may not plant flax and has no rights to the sycamore beams.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNA: If someone takes a field from his friend to work for a few years, he may not plant flax in it, and he has no rights to the sycamore beams.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens with a rule for a sharecropper who takes a field for a short time. He may not plant flax, and he may not cut the sycamore branches used for beams.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Flax weakens the soil badly, and a short-term worker would leave the owner with a damaged field. Sycamore branches take many years to grow back, so cutting them would take something that belongs to the owner's future. 'A few years' means fewer than seven.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה (the core text the גמרא discusses)
One who receives a field to work it, a sharecropper or tenant farmer
Flax, a crop that strongly drains the soil
Beams made from the branches of a sycamore tree
A few years, meaning fewer than seven

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who receives a field from his fellow to work it
for a few years,
may not plant it with flax,
and he has no rights to the sycamore beams.
phrases.notes: So he may not cut the sycamore's branches for himself, since they take years to grow back.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַמְקַבֵּל שָׂדֶה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ לְשָׁנִים מוּעָטוֹת
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A short-term sharecropper may not plant flax and may not take the sycamore beams.

steps.title: Seven-year sharecropper: flax in year one, and he may take the beams
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that someone who takes a field for seven years may plant flax in the first year and does have rights to the sycamore beams.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he took the field for seven years, he may plant flax in the first year, and he does have rights to the sycamore beams.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the opposite case, a long seven-year agreement. Here the sharecropper may plant flax in year one and may cut the sycamore beams.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With seven years, the soil has time to recover from flax planted in the first year. The sycamore branches also have time to grow back before he leaves. Either way, the owner gets back a field that is not damaged.

keyTerms.meaning: Seven years, the length of time that counts as a long agreement here

steps.whatToRemember: The dividing line is seven years. With fewer, he may not plant flax or take the beams. With seven, he may plant flax in year one and take the beams.

phrases.english: If he received it from him for seven years,
in the first year he may plant it with flax,
and he does have rights to the sycamore beams.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposite case to step 1: a long agreement instead of a short one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A seven-year sharecropper may plant flax in the first year and may take the sycamore beams.

steps.title: אביי: no beams, but he is paid for the tree's growth
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that a short-term sharecropper may not take the beams, but he is paid for the value the sycamore gained while he worked the field.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא: אביי said: He has no rights to the sycamore beams, but he does have rights to the growth of the sycamore.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with אביי, who adds a detail to the short-term case of the משנה. He may not cut the beams, but when he leaves he is paid for how much the tree grew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי separates two things: the beams themselves, which he may not take, and the added value (שבח) that grew during his time. The משנה only said 'no beams.' אביי reads that as leaving room for payment for the growth.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that analyzes the משנה
The added value of the sycamore, meaning its growth during the sharecropper's time

phrases.english: GEMARA: Abaye said:
To the sycamore beams he has no rights,
but to the growth of the sycamore he does have rights.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies how far the משנה's ruling of 'no beams' goes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A short-term sharecropper may not take the beams, but he is paid for the sycamore's growth.

steps.title: רבא: he is not even paid for the growth
steps.stepSummary: רבא disagrees with אביי and says the short-term sharecropper gets nothing for the sycamore, not even its growth.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: He does not even have rights to the growth of the sycamore.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא argues with אביי. In his view, the sharecropper has no claim at all on the sycamore, not even payment for its growth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא, the משנה's words 'he has no rights' cover everything about the sycamore. This sets up the argument that the גמרא tests next.

phrases.english: And Rava said: Even to the growth of the sycamore
he also has no rights.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרָבָא אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ בִּשְׁבַח שִׁקְמָה נָמֵי אֵין לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with אביי's position from step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The short-term sharecropper gets nothing for the sycamore, not even its growth.

steps.title: Challenge to רבא: the court appraises what he is owed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא from a ברייתא that says the court appraises what the departing sharecropper is owed, which seems to include the sycamore's growth.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: If someone takes a field from his friend and the time comes for him to leave, the court appraises what he is owed. Doesn't that mean they pay him for the growth of the sycamore?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to argue against רבא. It suggests that what the court 'appraises' must be the sycamore's growth, which is just what רבא denied.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says 'שמין לו' (they appraise for him) without saying what is being appraised. The גמרא suggests it means the growth of the trees, which would support אביי and contradict רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: They appraise for him, meaning the court figures out what he is owed
Isn't it that, a suggested reading meant to prove a point
His time to leave has arrived

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
phrases.notes: This challenge is aimed at רבא.

phrases.english: One who receives a field from his fellow
and his time to leave arrives,
they appraise for him.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי לָאו: שָׁמִין לוֹ בִּשְׁבַח שִׁקְמָה?
phrases.english: Is it not that they appraise for him the growth of the sycamore?

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: הַמְקַבֵּל שָׂדֶה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ וְהִגִּיעַ זְמַנּוֹ לָצֵאת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's position from step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's view that the sharecropper gets nothing for the sycamore's growth.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says the court appraises what the departing sharecropper is owed. That seems to mean the growth of the trees, which goes against רבא.

steps.title: Answer: the appraisal is for vegetables and beets
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends רבא: the ברייתא is talking about vegetables and beets still in the field, not the sycamore.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, they appraise for him the vegetables and beets.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading the ברייתא differently. The 'appraisal' is for vegetables and beets he planted, not for the sycamore.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once 'what is appraised' is read as vegetables, the ברייתא says nothing about the sycamore. רבא's view stands.

keyTerms.meaning: No, the start of a rejection

phrases.english: No, they appraise for him the vegetables and beets.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the source differently: the ברייתא is about a different item.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The court appraises the sycamore's growth, which goes against רבא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The court appraises only vegetables and beets left in the field, so רבא is fine.

steps.title: Challenge: why not just pull up the vegetables?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why vegetables would need an appraisal at all, since the sharecropper could simply pull them up and take them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Vegetables and beets? Let him pull them up and take them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges its own answer. If the issue is vegetables, he can just pull them out and take them with him, so why would the court need to appraise them?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Trees cannot be taken with him, so paying him makes sense for them. Vegetables can be harvested right away, so it seems an appraisal would be pointless. That makes the answer in step 6 look weak.

phrases.english: Vegetables and beets? Let him uproot them and take them!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the answer given in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the ברייתא's appraisal is about vegetables and beets.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Vegetables can be harvested and taken right away, so there is no need for the court to appraise them.

steps.title: Answer: market day has not come yet
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the case is when market day has not yet arrived, so pulling up the vegetables now would leave him unable to sell them.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where market day has not yet arrived.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: he cannot sell the vegetables yet because market day has not come. So instead of pulling them up, he leaves them and is paid their value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Uprooted vegetables would wilt before market day, so harvesting them now does not really help him. That is why the court appraises them for him. The ברייתא's appraisal is explained without the sycamore, and רבא's view stands.

keyTerms.meaning: In a case where it has not arrived

steps.whatToRemember: רבא holds that the short-term sharecropper gets nothing for the sycamore, not even its growth. The ברייתא's 'שמין לו' means vegetables still in the ground when market day has not yet come.

phrases.english: It is where market day has not yet arrived.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7 and protects the answer of step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a specific situation (before market day).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Vegetables could just be pulled up, so an appraisal would make no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: Before market day, pulling them up does him no good, so the court appraises them and pays him their value.

steps.title: A new ברייתא is brought against רבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא. Someone who received a field from another person reaches שביעית, and the court appraises what he is owed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone receives a field from his friend and the seventh year arrives, the court appraises it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is bringing a new source to challenge רבא again. This line only sets up the source; the actual attack comes a few steps later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the court makes an appraisal (שמין לו) for the man who has to leave the field. If that appraisal includes the sycamore's growth, it would go against רבא. But first the גמרא has to make sense of the ברייתא itself.

keyTerms.meaning: One who receives a field to farm for the owner
The seventh year, when the land rests
The court appraises the value owed to him

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who receives a field from his friend
and the seventh year arrived, they appraise it for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first ברייתא was explained as speaking about vegetables, a second ברייתא is brought against רבא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that the departing sharecropper gets nothing for the sycamore
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A court appraisal for someone leaving a field seems to include the growth he added.

steps.title: The seventh year does not take land away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how שביעית could end someone's hold on a field. It does not cancel his rights to the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does the seventh year take away the land?
steps.whatsHappening: Before using the ברייתא, the גמרא points out that its wording does not make sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שביעית makes the produce free for everyone, but the land itself stays with whoever holds it. So nobody is forced to leave the field, and there is nothing to appraise. The ברייתא's wording must be wrong.

phrases.english: Does the seventh year release the land?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording 'והגיע שביעית' in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שביעית does not remove a person from the land, so an appraisal makes no sense.

steps.title: Read it as the יובל instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the ברייתא to say יובל rather than שביעית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: If someone receives a field from his friend and the Jubilee year arrives, the court appraises it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the ברייתא's wording so that the year mentioned is one that does return fields.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the יובל, fields go back to their original owners. That would explain why the holder has to leave and why an appraisal is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say; the גמרא corrects the wording of a source
The fiftieth (Jubilee) year, when fields return to their original owners

phrases.english: Rather, say:
One who receives a field from his friend
and the Jubilee year arrived, they appraise it for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10 by changing שביעית to יובל.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the wording of the source
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא speaks about יובל, which does return fields.

steps.title: The יובל does not end a sharecropping deal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the יובל only returns fields that were sold, not fields given to a sharecropper.
steps.simpleTranslation: But still: does the Jubilee year cancel a sharecropping arrangement? The Torah says 'permanently'!
steps.whatsHappening: The corrected wording still has a problem, so the גמרא challenges it again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about 'לצמיתת' (selling permanently) shows that the יובל only cancels sales. A sharecropper (מקבל) never bought the field, so the יובל has nothing to cancel.

keyTerms.meaning: Permanently; the Torah's word for a full sale
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.english: But still, does the Jubilee release a sharecropping arrangement?
"Permanently," the Merciful One said!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the corrected wording from step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The corrected reading: a מקבל at the יובל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The יובל undoes only sales, so it has no effect on a sharecropper.

steps.title: Read it as a buyer, not a sharecropper
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the ברייתא again: it is about someone who bought a field and must return it at the יובל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: If someone buys a field from his friend and the Jubilee year arrives, the court appraises it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא changes the person in the ברייתא from a sharecropper to a buyer, so that the יובל really does take the field back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the case works: a buyer (לוקח) has to give the field back at the יובל, and the court appraises something for him. The next question is what exactly is being appraised.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
One who buys a field from his friend
and the Jubilee year arrived, they appraise it for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 12 by making the case a buyer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the wording of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא speaks about a sharecropper.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא speaks about a buyer, whose field the יובל returns.

steps.title: The appraisal must be for the sycamore's growth
steps.stepSummary: The appraisal cannot be for vegetables, because in the יובל they are הפקר. So it must be for the sycamore's שבח, which goes against רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that here too the court appraises vegetables and beets for him, that cannot be: vegetables and beets in the Jubilee year are ownerless! Rather, isn't it about the growth of the sycamore?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the ברייתא reads correctly, the גמרא makes its real attack on רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier (step 6), רבא's side explained that an appraisal was for vegetables. That answer cannot work here, because in the יובל produce is הפקר and belongs to no one. The only thing left to appraise is the sycamore's growth, so a person leaving a field does get paid for שבח.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say; it brings up a possible answer in order to reject it
Rather, is it not...? It pushes toward the only remaining explanation
The added value from the sycamore's growth

phrases.english: And if you would say so too here,
they appraise for him vegetables and beets?
phrases.notes: This is the same answer that worked for the earlier ברייתא in step 6.

phrases.english: Beets and vegetables in the Jubilee are ownerless!
Rather, is it not the growth of the sycamore!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: With the ברייתא now fixed, returns to the challenge against רבא that began in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that no payment is given for the sycamore's growth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Vegetables cannot be the subject because they are הפקר in the יובל, so the appraisal must be for the sycamore's growth.

steps.title: אביי explains: a special פסוק gives the buyer the growth
steps.stepSummary: אביי defends רבא: the buyer keeps the שבח only because a פסוק teaches that the field returns but the growth does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי explained it according to רבא: There it is different, because the verse says: 'And the sale of the house shall go out.' The thing sold goes back; the growth does not go back.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי, who disagrees with רבא, still answers the challenge for him by showing the ברייתא is a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says only the 'sale' (ממכר) goes back at the יובל. That means the improvement stays with the buyer. This is a Torah rule about יובל, not a proof that a sharecropper gets paid for growth.
steps.confusionAlert: אביי is the one who argued with רבא in this סוגיא, yet here he answers for רבא. He is showing that רבא's view can still stand.

phrases.english: Abaye explained it according to Rava:
There it is different, for the verse says:
"And the sale of the house shall go out."
The sale returns,
the growth does not return.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּרְגְּמַהּ אַבָּיֵי אַלִּיבָּא דְּרָבָא: שָׁאנֵי הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Special case based on a פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא shows that anyone leaving a field is paid for the growth.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a buyer at the יובל keeps the growth, because of a special פסוק.

steps.title: Why not learn a general rule from it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if a buyer keeps the שבח, why not apply the same rule to the sharecropper?
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us learn from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on אביי's answer by asking why the פסוק should not teach a rule for every case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah lets a buyer keep the growth, maybe that is the general rule, and the sharecropper should also be paid. That would bring back the challenge to רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: And let us learn from it

phrases.english: And let us learn from it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's answer in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's claim that the פסוק is limited to the יובל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A rule from a פסוק could be applied to similar cases, including the sharecropper.

steps.title: A buyer was a true owner; a sharecropper was not
steps.stepSummary: The cases are different: the buyer made a full purchase, and the יובל takes the field back by a royal decree, so he keeps what grew while it was his.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it was a complete sale, and the Jubilee is a release by the King.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the buyer's case cannot be copied, because the buyer really owned the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer fully owned the land until the יובל took it away by the King's (God's) decree. So whatever grew while he owned it is his. A sharecropper never owned the field, so רבא's ruling stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A release by the King; the Torah's decree takes the field back

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's view survives. A buyer keeps the שבח at the יובל because he was a true owner and the field is taken by the King's decree. A sharecropper was never an owner and gets nothing for the sycamore's growth.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that payment for improvements depends on whether the person owned the field, not just on who did the work.

phrases.english: There it is a full sale,
and the Jubilee is a release by the King.
phrases.notes: The 'King' is God; the field leaves the buyer by the Torah's decree, not because his ownership was weak.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 by showing the two cases are different.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer's rule applies to anyone leaving a field.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a true owner, whose field is taken by the King's decree, keeps the growth.

steps.title: רב פפא's hay field grows palm trees
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא took a field to grow hay. Palm trees sprouted in it, and when he left he asked the owners to pay him for this שבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא took land as a sharecropper to grow hay. Palm trees sprouted in it. When he was leaving, he said to the owners: Give me the value of the improvement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real story that tests the rule about an אריס and growth that happened on its own. This story sets up the questions that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, אביי and רבא argued about whether an אריס gets paid when a sycamore grows on its own. Here a real case comes up: palm trees grew on their own in a field meant for hay. רב פפא claims payment for the שבח.

keyTerms.meaning: Took land to work it, as a sharecropper or contractor
The improvement, the added value to the field

phrases.english: Rav Pappa received land for growing hay.
Palm trees sprouted in it.
When he was leaving,
he said to them: Give me the improvement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the theory about the buyer and the אריס, the גמרא brings a real case involving an אריס.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב פפא, as an אריס, claimed payment for palm trees that grew on their own in his hay field.

steps.title: Would you also claim growth of an existing palm tree?
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא challenges רב פפא: by your logic, if a palm tree in the field simply grew thicker, you would also want to be paid for that.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שישא, the son of רב אידי, said to רב פפא: If so, if there was a palm tree and it grew thick, would the master also want to be paid for its growth?
steps.whatsHappening: רב שישא attacks רב פפא's claim by pushing it to a result that sounds wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If an אריס gets paid for any growth in the field, then he should even be paid when an existing tree gets thicker. That sounds unreasonable. So רב פפא's claim seems to go too far.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, then... (introduces an unreasonable result)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי לְרַב פָּפָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi, said to Rav Pappa:
If so, a palm tree that grew thick,
would the master also want its improvement?
phrases.notes: "The master" is a polite way of saying "you," meaning רב פפא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's claim from step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's claim to be paid for trees that grew on their own
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reductio: by that logic, an אריס would be paid even when an existing palm grew thicker, which is unreasonable.

steps.title: It depends on what the sharecropper expected
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers: in the palm-tree case the אריס did not come in expecting that growth, but I did come in expecting to share in improvements.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, the sharecropper did not come down to the field with that in mind. Here, I came down with this in mind.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא defends himself by showing that the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With an existing palm tree, the אריס only expects to share its fruit, not its growth. רב פפא says that in his deal he did expect to share in new growth on the land. So the result depends on what was expected when he took the field.

keyTerms.meaning: With this in mind, expecting this
Went down, entered into the field or deal

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם לָאו אַדַּעְתָּא דְּהָכִי נָחֵית,
phrases.english: He said to him: There, he did not go down with this in mind,
I, here, went down with this in mind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב שישא's challenge in step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between cases based on what the sharecropper expected
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any growth in the field, even a tree getting thicker, earns the אריס a share.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only growth the אריס expected to share in when he took the field earns payment.

steps.title: Does רב פפא follow אביי?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose opinion רב פפא follows, and suggests it is אביי, who says an אריס gets the שבח of a sycamore.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like whom did he rule? Like אביי, who said: He has a share in the improvement of the sycamore.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא connects this story to the earlier argument between אביי and רבא. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי said an אריס gets a share of a sycamore's growth, and רבא said he does not. רב פפא's claim seems to match אביי. That would mean רב פפא disagrees with רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: Like whom? Whose opinion does this follow?

phrases.english: Like whom?
Like Abaye, who said:
He has a share in the improvement of the sycamore.
phrases.notes: This is the earlier argument: אביי says the אריס shares in the sycamore's growth, and רבא says he does not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Links רב פפא's claim back to the אביי and רבא argument.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב פפא's claim only fits אביי's view and not רבא's.

steps.title: It even fits רבא, because here there was a loss
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects that idea: even רבא could agree, because with the sycamore the אריס lost nothing, but here the palm trees took up hay space.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say he follows רבא. There, the sharecropper has no loss. Here, there is a loss.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion that רב פפא must follow אביי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא denies payment in the sycamore case only because the אריס lost nothing there. In רב פפא's field, the palm trees took up land he could have used for hay. That is a real loss, so even רבא would agree he should be paid.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the key test for the rest of the section: payment for growth depends on whether the אריס suffered a loss.

phrases.english: You can even say it follows Rava,
there, he has no loss.
Here, there is a loss.
phrases.notes: The palm trees grew on land he could have used for his hay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the claim in step 21 that רב פפא must follow אביי.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that רב פפא's claim only fits אביי
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It missed a difference: here the אריס suffered a loss, and in the sycamore case he did not.

steps.title: Your loss is only a handful of hay
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא argues that רב פפא's loss is tiny: just a handful of hay. So he should take that and go.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What did you lose? A handful of hay. Take a handful of hay and go!
steps.whatsHappening: רב שישא challenges רב פפא again, this time on the size of his loss.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if there is a loss, the owner only owes what was actually lost. That is a small amount of hay, not the full value of the palm trees.

phrases.english: He said to him: What did you lose?
A handful of hay,
take a handful of hay and go!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts that payment depends on a loss, but says the loss is tiny.
steps.kashyaTarget: The amount רב פפא is claiming
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Payment should match the actual loss, which is only a handful of hay, not the value of the trees.

steps.title: I grew expensive saffron there
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that he grew garden saffron, so his loss was much more than hay.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I was growing garden saffron.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers that his loss was not small.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He used the field for valuable saffron, not only hay. So the trees took the place of expensive produce, and his loss was large.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנָא כּוּרְכְּמָא רִישְׁקָא רַבַּאי.
phrases.english: He said to him: I grew garden saffron.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 23 that the loss was small.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual correction about the size of the loss
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The loss was only a handful of cheap hay.

steps.title: You showed you planned to leave, so you get only wood value
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא says: by growing saffron, you showed you planned to take your crop and leave. So take your saffron, and for the trees you get only their value as wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You revealed that you meant to take your crop and leave. Take your garden saffron and go. You get only the value of the wood.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שישא turns רב פפא's own answer against him and gives the final outcome of this story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saffron is a short-term crop. It shows רב פפא planned to harvest and leave, not to raise trees. So he cannot claim the trees' growth value as a long-term partner. He gets only what the trees are worth as cut wood.

keyTerms.meaning: The value of the trees as wood

steps.whatToRemember: In רב פפא's case, the final outcome is that he gets only the trees' wood value. His own plan to grow a short-term crop showed he never expected to share in the trees' growth.

phrases.english: He said to him: You revealed your intention
that you acted in order to take your crop and leave –
take the garden saffron and go,

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לְךָ אֶלָּא דְּמֵי עֵצִים בִּלְבַד.
phrases.english: you have nothing but the value of the wood alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב פפא's saffron answer from step 24, using his own claim from step 20 about what he expected.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רב פפא's claim to the full growth value
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Growing a short-term crop shows he never expected to share in long-term tree growth.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב פפא gets only the value of the trees as wood.

steps.title: רב ביבי's field grows trees
steps.stepSummary: רב ביבי בר אביי took a field and built an earth fence around it. Trees sprouted, and when he left he asked to be paid for the שבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ביבי בר אביי took land to work and surrounded it with an earth fence. Trees sprouted in it. When he was leaving, he said to the owners: Give me my improvement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story with a similar claim. This sets up רב פפי's response in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like רב פפא, רב ביבי asks to be paid for trees that grew on their own. The question is whether רב פפא's reasoning helps him.

keyTerms.meaning: A fence or bank made of earth

phrases.aramaic: רַב בִּיבִי בַּר אַבָּיֵי קַבֵּיל אַרְעָא
phrases.english: Rav Beivai bar Abaye received land
and surrounded it with an earth fence,
trees sprouted in it.
When he was leaving, he said to them:
Give me my improvement.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב בִּיבִי בַּר אַבָּיֵי קַבֵּיל אַרְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second real case, parallel to רב פפא's story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב ביבי claimed payment for trees that grew on their own in the field he worked.

steps.title: No loss, so no payment
steps.stepSummary: רב פפי sharply rejects רב ביבי's claim. רב פפא only claimed payment because he had a loss, and רב ביבי had none.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפי said: Because you come from unfortunate people, you say unfortunate words?! Even רב פפא said this only when he had a loss. Here, what loss do you have?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפי rejects רב ביבי's claim, using the loss rule from רב פפא's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule from step 22 is that the אריס is paid for growth only if he suffered a loss. רב ביבי's trees did not take the place of any crop of his. So he lost nothing and gets nothing.
steps.whatToRemember: An אריס can claim payment for trees that grew on their own only if they caused him a real loss. If he lost nothing, as with רב ביבי, he gets nothing.

phrases.english: Rav Pappi said:
Because you come from unfortunate people,
phrases.notes: A sharp jab: אביי's family came from עלי's family, whose descendants were cursed to die young.

phrases.english: you say unfortunate words?!
Even Rav Pappa said this only
where he has a loss,
here, what loss do you have?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲפִילּוּ רַב פָּפָּא לָא אֲמַר אֶלָּא דְּאִית לֵיהּ פְּסֵידָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב ביבי's claim in step 26 using the loss rule from step 22.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: He treated רב פפא's case as a precedent but ignored the key condition: a real loss.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Without a loss, an אריס gets nothing for growth that happened on its own.

steps.title: רב יוסף and the five sons-in-law of his planter
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף's planter died and left five sons-in-law. רב יוסף worried they would each rely on the others and the work would suffer. So he told them: take your payment for the improvement and leave, or I will remove you with nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף had a planter who died and left five sons-in-law. רב יוסף said: Until now I dealt with one person. Now there are five. Until now nobody leaned on anyone else, and I had no loss. Now five people will each lean on the others, and I will lose. He told them: If you take payment for your improvement and leave, good. If not, I will remove you without payment for the improvement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story: רב יוסף wants to end his deal with his dead planter's five heirs, and he gives them an ultimatum.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is shared responsibility. When five people share a job, each assumes another will do it, and the field suffers. So רב יוסף offers them full payment if they leave willingly, and threatens to remove them with nothing if they refuse.

keyTerms.meaning: A planter: a worker who plants trees in someone else's field in exchange for a share
They rely on each other (each leaves the work for the others)
The improvement (the added value) the planter brought to the field

phrases.aramaic: רַב יוֹסֵף הֲוָה לֵיהּ הָהוּא שַׁתָּלָא,
phrases.english: Rav Yosef had a certain planter.
He died and left five sons-in-law.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר עַד הָאִידָּנָא חַד, הַשְׁתָּא חַמְשָׁה.
phrases.english: He said: Until now, one; now, five.
phrases.notes: He means: until now I dealt with one worker, and now I have to deal with five.

phrases.aramaic: עַד הָאִידָּנָא לָא הֲווֹ סָמְכוּ אַהֲדָדֵי
phrases.english: Until now they did not rely on each other
and did not cause me a loss;

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא חַמְשָׁה סָמְכוּ אַהֲדָדֵי וּמַפְסְדוּ לִי.
phrases.english: now the five will rely on each other and cause me a loss.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אִי שָׁקְלִיתוּ שְׁבָחַיְיכוּ וּמִסְתַּלְּקִיתוּ – מוּטָב,
phrases.english: He said to them: If you take your improvement and leave, good;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לָא – מְסַלֵּיקְנָא לְכוּ בְּלָא שְׁבָחָא.
phrases.english: and if not, I will remove you without the improvement.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יוֹסֵף הֲוָה לֵיהּ הָהוּא שַׁתָּלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about removing a planter, continuing the theme of paying for שבח from the stories before it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An owner may remove a dead planter's heirs. If they refuse to leave with payment, he threatens to remove them without payment for the שבח.

steps.title: The source for רב יוסף's threat
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף gives the source for his threat. רב יהודה (or רב הונא, or רב נחמן) ruled that when a planter dies, his heirs may be removed without payment for the improvement.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רב יהודה said (some say it was רב הונא, and some say רב נחמן): When a planter dies, we remove his heirs without payment for the improvement.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף cites a ruling that backs up רב יוסף's threat to remove the heirs with nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling says that once a planter dies, the owner may remove his heirs, and he does not even owe them the value of the improvement. That is why רב יוסף felt he could threaten them. Tosafot explain that he named just one of these rabbis, and later students weren't sure which one, so all three names are given. The very next step rejects this ruling.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב הוּנָא,
phrases.english: For Rav Yehuda said, and some say it was Rav Huna,
and some say it was Rav Nachman:
This planter who died, his heirs
we remove them without the improvement.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording, 'we remove them.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב הוּנָא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the legal basis for רב יוסף's threat in step 28.
steps.raayaObject: רב יוסף's threat to remove the heirs without payment for the שבח
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling of רב יהודה (or רב הונא, or רב נחמן) that a dead planter's heirs are removed without שבח

steps.title: That ruling is not the הלכה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a short comment: the ruling about removing the heirs without payment is not correct.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this is not correct.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the ruling it just quoted. The heirs cannot be thrown out with nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא states that the הלכה does not follow the ruling from step 29, so heirs may not be removed with nothing. That weakens the second half of רב יוסף's threat, the part about removing them without payment.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is not correct (literally, 'it is not a thing')

steps.confusionAlert: Only the ruling about removing heirs with no payment is rejected here. The story itself, where רב יוסף offered them payment to leave, still stands.

phrases.english: But this is not correct.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the ruling quoted in step 29.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The halacha that a dead planter's heirs are removed without שבח
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The הלכה does not follow this view. The heirs keep their right to the שבח.

steps.title: A planter who promised to leave if he caused a loss
steps.stepSummary: A planter promised: if I cause a loss, I will leave. He did cause a loss. רב יהודה rules that he leaves without payment for the improvement.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain planter told the owners: If I cause a loss, I will leave. He caused a loss. רב יהודה said: He leaves without payment for the improvement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new case about a planter's promise, and gives רב יהודה's ruling. This opens a disagreement that continues in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The planter promised only to leave. He said nothing about giving up his payment. רב יהודה reads the promise as also giving up his share in the improvement, so he goes away with nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: I cause a loss (damage the field)

phrases.english: A certain planter who said to them:
If I cause a loss, I will leave.
He caused a loss.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: מִסְתַּלַּק בְּלָא שְׁבָחָא.
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: He leaves without the improvement.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא שַׁתָּלָא דַּאֲמַר לְהוּ: אִי מַפְסֵדְינָא מִסְתַּלַּקְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case about planters and שבח.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רב יהודה, a planter who promised to leave if he caused a loss, and then did, leaves without שבח.

steps.title: רב כהנא: he leaves, but takes his payment
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא disagrees with רב יהודה. The planter leaves, but he still gets paid for the improvement. רב כהנא agrees, though, that if the planter said 'I will leave without the improvement,' he gets nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: He leaves and takes payment for the improvement. But רב כהנא agrees that if the planter said, 'If I cause a loss I will leave without the improvement,' then he leaves without the improvement.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion: רב כהנא reads the planter's promise narrowly. He promised to leave, not to give up his payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב כהנא, everything depends on what the planter actually said. 'I will leave' means only leaving. Only if he clearly said 'without the improvement' does he lose it. This shows that רב כהנא accepts that such a promise binds the planter when it is said explicitly.

keyTerms.meaning: And he agrees (in this case, even though he disagrees elsewhere)

phrases.aramaic: רַב כָּהֲנָא אָמַר: מִסְתַּלַּק וְשָׁקֵיל שְׁבָחָא.
phrases.english: Rav Kahana said: He leaves and takes the improvement.
And Rav Kahana agrees that if he said:
'If I cause a loss, I will leave without the improvement,'
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets belong to the corrected wording, so read it as 'מַפְסֵידְנָא', 'I cause a loss.'

phrases.english: he leaves without the improvement.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא אָמַר: מִסְתַּלַּק וְשָׁקֵיל שְׁבָחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב יהודה's ruling in step 31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'I will leave' does not mean giving up the שבח. Only an explicit 'without the שבח' takes it away.

steps.title: רבא: the promise is an אסמכתא
steps.stepSummary: רבא says such a promise is an אסמכתא: a promise the planter made without really expecting to have to keep it. An אסמכתא does not bind him, so he keeps his payment for the improvement.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is an אסמכתא, and an אסמכתא does not make a binding transfer.
steps.whatsHappening: A third opinion: רבא says the planter's promise has no legal force at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The planter was sure he would not cause a loss, so he never seriously meant to give anything up. רבא calls this an אסמכתא, which does not transfer anything. So even if he said 'without the improvement,' he still gets paid. That goes further than רב כהנא.

keyTerms.meaning: A conditional promise made without real intent to pay, because the person is confident the condition won't happen
Does not transfer ownership (is not binding)

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule that אסמכתא לא קניא shows up all over ש״ס, especially with gambling and penalty clauses. Here it protects the planter from losing his earned improvement.

phrases.english: Rava said: It is an asmachta,
and an asmachta does not effect a transfer.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: אַסְמַכְתָּא הִיא, וְאַסְמַכְתָּא לָא קָנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with both רב יהודה and רב כהנא by saying the promise is not binding at all.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A planter's promise to give up his שבח if he causes a loss is an אסמכתא and does not bind him.

steps.title: Challenge to רבא from the sharecropper's promise in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא. A משנה teaches that a sharecropper who says 'If I leave the field unworked, I will pay with the best produce' must keep his word. Why is that not an אסמכתא too?
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבא, how is this different from what we learned in a משנה: 'If I leave the field fallow and don't work it, I will pay with the best'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבא with a משנה where a similar 'if I fail' promise does bind the worker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two cases look the same. In both, a worker promises a penalty if he fails. If the משנה makes the sharecropper pay, then a promise like this should not count as a non-binding אסמכתא. That seems to contradict רבא.

phrases.english: And according to Rava, what is the difference
from that which we learned in a mishnah:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה earlier in this perek, on 104a.

phrases.aramaic: אִם אוֹבִיר וְלָא אַעֲבֵיד אֲשַׁלֵּם בְּמֵיטְבָא!
phrases.english: 'If I leave it fallow and do not work it, I will pay with the best'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's ruling in step 33.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that a promise like this is an אסמכתא and not binding
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה makes a sharecropper keep a similar conditional penalty promise, so such promises seem to be binding.

steps.title: Paying for real damage versus losing everything
steps.stepSummary: There is a difference. In the משנה, the sharecropper pays only for the damage he actually caused, so it is not an אסמכתא. Here too we take off the actual damage, but we pay the planter the rest of his improvement.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he pays for the loss he caused. Here, we take off the loss he caused, and we give him the rest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבא: paying for real damage is fair and binding, but losing everything beyond that is an אסמכתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sharecropper in the משנה pays exactly what he damaged, which is just honest compensation. The planter here is being asked to lose his whole improvement, much more than the damage. So רבא's rule is that we take off only the true loss, and the rest still belongs to the planter.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, a planter who causes a loss keeps his שבח. We only subtract the actual damage. A promise to lose more than the real damage is an אסמכתא and not binding.

phrases.english: There, what he caused to be lost, he pays;
here, what he caused to be lost, we deduct from him,
and the rest we give to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge to רבא in step 34.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sharecropper's promise in the משנה seemed to prove that all such promises are binding.
steps.terutzMaskana: Paying for the actual damage is binding. Losing more than that, like the whole שבח, is an אסמכתא. So the planter pays for the damage and gets the rest.

steps.title: רבינא removes his planter, and רבא approves
steps.stepSummary: רוניא, רבינא's planter, caused a loss, so רבינא removed him. רוניא complained to רבא, and רבא said רבינא did the right thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רוניא was רבינא's planter, and he caused a loss. רבינא removed him. רוניא came before רבא and said: 'Look at what he did to me!' רבא told him: 'He did well.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case of a planter who caused damage and was sent away. רבא rules that the owner was right to remove him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier steps dealt with a planter who made a promise to leave if he caused a loss. Here no such promise is mentioned, yet רבא still says the owner was right to remove him because he caused a loss. This shows that causing a loss is enough reason to send this kind of worker away.

keyTerms.meaning: A planter: a worker hired to plant and care for a field
He removed him, sent him away
He did well, he acted correctly

phrases.english: Runya was the planter of Ravina.
He caused a loss. He (Ravina) removed him.
He (Runya) came before Rava.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ חֲזִי מָר מַאי קָא עָבֵיד לִי!
phrases.english: He said to him: Let the master see what he has done to me!
He (Rava) said to him: He did well.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the theoretical discussion of a planter's promise, the גמרא brings a practical case of a planter who caused a loss.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An owner may remove a planter who caused a loss; רבא says the owner acted correctly.

steps.title: The planter protests that he was never warned
steps.stepSummary: רוניא objects to רבא's ruling: רבינא never warned him before removing him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רוניא said to רבא: 'But he never warned me!'
steps.whatsHappening: The planter pushes back against רבא's ruling. He argues it is unfair to send him away without first being warned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רוניא's claim is that a worker should get a warning before being fired, so he has a chance to fix his ways. The challenge is aimed at the fairness of removing him suddenly.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָא לֹא הִתְרָה בִּי!
phrases.english: He (Runya) said to him: But he did not warn me!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָא לֹא הִתְרָה בִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to רבא's ruling in step 36.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that רבינא acted correctly by removing the planter.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A worker should be warned before he is removed; since no warning was given, removing him seems unjustified.

steps.title: רבא: no warning is needed
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that in this case the owner did not have to warn the planter first.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: 'You did not need to be warned.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the planter's protest. He says a warning was not required here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא does not accept that a warning is always needed. For this type of worker, causing a loss is enough reason to remove him right away. The next step shows this is part of a wider rule רבא holds.

keyTerms.meaning: To be warned, to give a warning

phrases.english: He (Rava) said to him: You did not need to be warned.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the words in round brackets, 'it is not necessary to warn'; the words in square brackets are the corrected wording. Both mean the same.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the planter's protest in step 37.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects the assumption that a warning is required
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A worker must be warned before he can be removed.
steps.terutzMaskana: For this kind of worker, no warning is needed before removing him after he caused a loss.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא rules that a planter who caused a loss may be removed even without a prior warning.

steps.title: רבא's general rule about certain workers begins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says רבא's ruling fits his own view, and begins quoting his rule about a children's teacher, a planter, a slaughterer, and a bloodletter.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא follows his own reasoning, for רבא said: A teacher of children, a planter, a slaughterer, and a bloodletter...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רבא's answer to רוניא matches a general rule רבא taught elsewhere. This line is a setup: it lists the workers, and the rule about them comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase רבא לטעמיה tells us this was not a one-time decision but part of רבא's consistent approach. The list groups the planter together with other workers whose mistakes can cause serious harm. What רבא says about all of them continues in the next part of the text.

keyTerms.meaning: Following his own reasoning, consistent with his own view

phrases.english: Rava follows his own line of reasoning,
as Rava said:
a teacher of children, a planter, a ritual slaughterer, and a bloodletter,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains that רבא's answer in step 38 matches a general rule he holds, and begins quoting it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא has a general rule that groups a children's teacher, a planter, a slaughterer, and a bloodletter together; the rule itself continues in the next text.
